Rao’s Case study · October 2026

Product Design Edition · Three.js

A jar you can spin, and a name spelled in sauce.

A flat label mock-up became an interactive, glass-real 3D jar. Then it learned one party trick: it pours itself over a single strand of spaghetti until the sauce spells Raveena. It ships as one file you can email.

Format
Interactive web piece, WebGL
Built with
three.js, Canvas 2D, a little GLSL
Made
One afternoon, design-led pairing with Claude Code
Ships as
A single 1 MB HTML file that works offline

01 · The brief

Three asks, each one bolder.

The work arrived as three short prompts. Each built on the one before, and each was steered by reacting to a live, running build rather than to specs or mock-ups.

Ask 1
Using three.js create a 3d model of this in a small website. Make it AMAZING, and shiny like a real jar.

Input: one flat product shot of a parody label. Bar: it has to read as real glass.

Ask 2
Make a button that spills the sauce on a single spaghetti noodle, and then it zooms out, and it spells Raveena with the sauce.

A one-button story with a reveal: the payoff only lands if the word is hidden until the camera pulls back.

Ask 3
Now I want that all zipped up in a single index.html file so I can send it to someone named Raveena.

The audience is one person on an unknown device, with no install, no server and possibly no internet.

02 · How we worked

Build it, look at it, fix what you see.

We skipped formal planning on purpose: the direction was to build and show. Every change was checked in a live browser preview, and every fix below came from looking at a real render rather than guessing.

01

Reference

Crop the portrait from the photo and treat the label as the design system.

02

Model

Turn the jar’s outline into 3D, then add the label, lid and sauce.

03

Light

Build a photo studio from glowing panels so the glass has something to reflect.

04

Look-dev

Screenshot, critique, adjust, repeat. Eight rounds on the base jar.

05

Choreograph

Write the spill as an 18-second shot list, then make code follow it.

06

Ship

Inline everything into one file and prove it needs nothing else.

03 · The jar

From a flat photo to real glass.

Shape before surface

The glass is one continuous outline spun around a centre line, so the shoulder, the ribs at the neck and the rolled lip come out as a single smooth surface. The sauce, label and lid are separate shapes nested just inside or outside it.

A label worth turning round for

The front panel faithfully reproduces the reference. The sides didn’t exist, so we wrote them: a “From Our Studio” recipe whose ingredients include whole peeled user research, and a “Design Facts” panel (Delight 120%, Jargon 0g) in the shape of a nutrition label. All of it is drawn in code, so it stays sharp up close.

Why it looks like glass

The glass bends light, has a glossy coat and splits colour very slightly at its edges. Behind it, the sauce has its own wet sheen and flecks of basil and pepper, so you read depth through the wall.

Shine needs something to reflect

The “studio” is a ring of large glowing panels built in the scene, with no photo files. Two arrangements give two moods: cool Studio and warm Golden hour. A mirrored copy of the jar under a dark floor provides the reflection.

04 · The look-dev loop

Every fix started with a screenshot.

These are the real in-progress captures from the session, kept at their original preview size.

The invisible jar

The first load showed the page but no jar. The preview window measured zero pixels wide at the very first frame, so the 3D view was set up at size zero. Guarding every size against zero brought the jar back.

Gravel, not purée

The sauce read as crushed gravel and the paper glowed white. Blurring the sauce texture made it a purée; a warm tint and less sheen turned the label back into cream paper.

The grey haze

The floor caught the overhead softbox and washed out the whole scene. We hid parts of the scene one at a time to find the culprit, then made the floor itself unlit and let the mirrored jar do the reflecting.

Pink sauce

With the lid off, the sauce faced straight up into the brightest light and turned pink. It got its own calmer material, so the surface stays deep red.

05 · The spill

One noodle. One unbroken line.

A noodle can’t lift off the floor between letters, so the word had to be one continuous stroke. Regular fonts are outlines, which would give us the edges of the letters, not a path down their middle. We needed a single-line script font, the kind pen plotters use.

0:04 · Close-up

Hide the word

The camera dives down beside the noodle before the pour starts. At this distance it’s just a strand of spaghetti, and that’s the point: the shape can’t give the reveal away.

0:07 · Coat

Make the sauce behave

The sauce lands as a small bead and swells out along the noodle over the next second, like a real pour settling. Droplets splash out and stay where they fall.

0:10 · Pull back

The reveal

Mid-pour, the camera rises and pulls away while the jar keeps tracing. The last letters are still bare noodle, so you watch the word finish.

0:12 · Finish

Land the last stroke

The jar tilts back, the stream thins and breaks from the lip, and the final drop falls onto the tail of the a.

0:18 · Hero

Back to a product shot

The jar returns home, the lid hops back on and screws shut, and the camera settles on the jar with the name laid out in front of it.

06 · The shot list

Directed like a film, to the tenth of a second.

The whole spill runs from a single timeline. Jar, lid, stream and camera each read the same clock, which is why the overlaps feel deliberate.

07 · Under the hood

The small things that sell it.

Noodle

Over, not through

Wherever the word crosses itself, the noodle finds the earlier strand and rises smoothly over it instead of passing through. Cursive crosses itself a lot.

Sauce

Built once, revealed live

The full sauce trail exists from the start, shrunk to nothing. A tiny graphics program swells each section as the pour reaches it, so it grows smoothly with no stutter.

Stream

A pour that lags

The stream curves out of the lip and down to the noodle. The jar follows the word with a slight delay, so the stream leans like a real pour.

Camera

Zoom that feels even

The pull-back eases its distance on a curve rather than a straight line, so going from close-up to wide feels like one steady move instead of a lurch.

Jar

Label toward camera

As it tips, the jar also turns half a circle so the label faces the camera through the pour, then turns the rest of the way on the way home.

Reflection

A mirror that keeps up

The reflected jar is rebuilt from the real one every frame, so the reflection stays correct even mid-flight and upside down.

08 · Shipping it

One file, for one person.

For the final ask, everything was folded into a single HTML file: the three.js library, the code, the portrait, the word path and the four typefaces. The check was simple: open it, play the spill, and confirm the page loaded nothing from anywhere else.

1 fileDouble-click to open, works offline
1 MBIncluding the full 3D library
11Font styles embedded, so the label looks the same everywhere
18 sFrom button press to the final shot

09 · What we learned

Notes for next time.

i

Look before you tune. Most of the visual problems weren’t where they first seemed. Hiding things one at a time found the real cause faster than adjusting sliders.

ii

Design the reveal, then the effect. The spill works because the camera keeps the word hidden until it pulls back. That was decided before any sauce existed.

iii

The right font is a technical choice. The single-line script font made one unbroken noodle possible, and choosing it settled half the problem.

iv

Ship for the actual audience. “Send it to Raveena” meant one file and no setup, which shaped the final step more than any feature did.

For Raveena, with sauce.
